newsitem.title: USA: GREENSPAN: Won't use interest rates to weaken shares.
newsitem.headline: GREENSPAN: Won't use interest rates to weaken shares.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Wednesday that the central bank was not out to deflate the stock market by boosting interest rates.
"We don't view monetary policy as a tool to ... prick the stock market bubble or something like that," Greenspan told a House Banking subcommittee.
But the Fed chief made clear that the central bank would take account of the level of the stock market, among other factors, in deciding whether to change short-term rates.
His comments helped spark a steep run-up on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares soared 93.13 points, or 1.36 percent, to close at 6,945.85.
Financial markets have been on edge since Greenspan suggested last week that equity prices might be too high because of investors' "irrational exuberance."
The Fed chief has come in for some criticism for those comments from investors and analysts who have accused him of meddling in the market.
Lawmakers joined in the attack on the Fed chief on Wednesday at the second and last stage of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress on the economy.

In his testimony to Congress and in a speech to business economists earlier on Wednesday, Greenspan acknowledged that he was not sure where the stock market was headed but he did not back away from his remarks suggesting that prices may be too high.
"I don't know what the stock price outlook is," he said.
If Wall Street analysts' forecasts of corporate earnings are right, then the stock market is properly priced, he said. But if they are not, the market is in for some problems.

"It's pretty obvious that if you look at a normal pricing model for stocks, what you get is a not unreasonable level of prices if the earnings forecasts which the analysts are publishing are accurate," Greenspan said.

The accuracy of those earnings forecasts in turn hinges on whether corporate profit margins continue to rise. Margins are "quite high" when compared with 1991, but are significantly below levels that prevailed in the 1960s, when inflation was last around current low levels, he said.
"Is it possible for margins to rise further?" Greenspan asked. "It certainly is.
"If, however, profit margins ... don't go any further, then the market will run into some difficulty," he added.
As he did on Tuesday, the central bank chief defended his cautionary comments on equity prices and again denied that he was trying to talk the high-flying stock market down.
"You cannot affect the broad level of equity values by jawboning," he said, adding: "There is no way you can talk down or talk up prices or interest rates."
Greenspan argued that the Fed needs to take account of what he called "balance sheet forces" because of their increasing importance in trying to gauge the future direction of the economy.

The Fed is concerned about the run-up in stock prices, Greenspan made clear last week in testimony to a Senate panel, because it could be a harbinger of faster inflation ahead and could damage the economy if stocks abruptly reversed.
Greenspan told the business economists that markets, especially the stock market, very rarely "peak out" in response to any particular event.
"What tends to happen is that everyone gets increasingly bullish and everyone is committed and there's no one left to buy when somebody wants to sell," he said.

"The trouble is that the person who is standing next to the market and sneezes at the time that that market turns is going to find out that his sneeze caused the price ... to fall," Greenspan added in what could be seen as a reference to himself and his recent comments.
